lessons.title: Natural Fibres: Cotton, Linen, Silk and Wool
lessons.content:
Textiles begin as fibres, and every fibre is either natural or man-made. Natural fibres come from plants or animals and are classified accordingly: cotton, linen, jute, coir and sisal are cellulosic plant fibres, while wool and silk are protein animal fibres. Cotton grows in the boll of the cotton plant, is spun from staple fibres and is the most used textile in the world; linen comes from the stem of the flax plant; wool is the fleece of sheep; and silk is a continuous filament reeled from the cocoon of the silkworm. A fibre's origin determines its properties, and its properties determine what it is good for.

Cotton is strong, absorbent, cool to wear, soft, cheap and easy to wash, which is why it is used for school uniforms, shirts, underwear and bed linen, and why it is comfortable in Caribbean heat. It creases badly, shrinks unless pre-shrunk, dries slowly and mildews if stored damp. Linen is even more absorbent and cooler than cotton, stronger when wet, lint-free and luxurious, but it creases very badly and is expensive, so it appears in summer wear, table linen and suits. Wool is warm, elastic, resilient and absorbent, and it does not crease, but it felts and shrinks with heat, agitation and alkalis, and is damaged by moths, so it is hand-washed or dry-cleaned and used for suits, school sweaters and blankets. Silk is the strongest natural fibre, lustrous, soft and drapes beautifully, but it is expensive, sun-fades, water-spots, and needs gentle hand-washing.

Caribbean growers and makers also work with other natural fibres: coir from coconut husk for mats and brushes, sisal for rope and bags, jute for sacking, and in some islands sea island cotton, which has longer, finer staples than ordinary cotton and is prized for luxury shirts. Knowing fibre properties lets a maker choose correctly for climate and purpose - absorbent and cool for heat, warm and resilient for cool, strong and lint-free for wear - and lets a consumer read a label and predict how a garment will wash, wear and last.
objectives: Classify natural fibres by origin and state their properties
Match fibre properties to appropriate uses
Identify Caribbean natural fibres and their products

experiment.description: Fibre Sorter: Sort fibres into plant and animal, then match each to its properties and best uses.

lessons.title: Man-made Fibres, Blends and Fabric Construction
lessons.content:
Man-made fibres are produced by people, either from natural polymers or from synthetic chemicals. Regenerated fibres are made by dissolving a natural polymer and re-forming it into filaments: viscose rayon, acetate and modal from wood pulp, and lyocell from wood pulp in a cleaner closed-loop process. Synthetic fibres are built from petrochemicals: polyester, nylon, acrylic and elastane (spandex). Their properties differ sharply from natural fibres: they are strong, light, quick-drying, resistant to creasing, moths and mildew, and cheap; but they are less absorbent, so they feel hot and clammy against the skin in humid heat, they hold static and oily stains, and they melt rather than burn, which is a safety issue. Elastane gives stretch, which is why it appears in swimwear, sportswear and jeans.

Blends combine fibres to gain the best of each. Polycotton mixes polyester with cotton for strength, crease resistance and quicker drying at the cost of some absorbency, and is used in uniforms and easy-care shirting. Polywool blends add durability and crease recovery to wool. Tricel-and-polyester blends give permanent pleats and are used in school skirts. Blends are identified by burning tests, microscopy and chemical tests, because the way a blended fabric behaves is a compromise between its component fibres and this affects care.

Fibres become fabric by several routes. Woven fabrics interlace warp and weft yarns on a loom, giving stability and little stretch; the plain weave is the simplest and strongest, the twill weave (as in denim) is hard-wearing, and the satin weave is smooth and lustrous. Knitted fabrics loop yarns together (weft knitting as in T-shirts, warp knitting as in swimwear), giving stretch, drape and warmth. Non-woven fabrics are bonded fibres or webs, used in interfacing, disposable items and wadding. Fabrics also receive finishes: mercerising improves cotton's lustre and strength, sanforising prevents shrinkage, flame retardants and water repellents add safety and function, and dyeing, printing and embossing add colour and pattern. Choosing a fabric therefore means choosing a fibre, a construction and a finish - each of which changes how the fabric sews, hangs, washes and lasts.
objectives: Describe regenerated and synthetic fibres with their properties
Explain why fibres are blended and identify common blends
Distinguish woven, knitted and non-woven fabrics and describe common finishes

experiment.description: Fabric Lab: Choose fibres to build a blend, then see the resulting properties and the fabric's best use.

lessons.title: Laundering, Stain Removal, Care Labels and Storage
lessons.content:
Good care begins with reading the label. Care labelling uses five symbols - washing (a washtub with a temperature or dots), bleaching (a triangle), drying (a square with a circle for tumble drying), ironing (an iron with dots for temperature) and professional care (a circle with a letter for dry cleaning) - and any symbol crossed through means do not do that. The fibre and blend usually determine the treatment: cotton and linen take hot water, strong detergent and a hot iron; wool and silk need cool water, mild detergent, no wringing and a cool iron; polyester, nylon and acrylic need warm water and a cool iron because they melt; and garments with elastane should not be tumble-dried on high heat.

Laundering is a sequence, not a single act: sort by colour, fabric and degree of soil; empty pockets, mend tears, remove trimmings; pre-treat stains and collars; wash with the right amount of detergent at the right temperature and load size; rinse thoroughly to avoid residue, which yellows whites and dulls colour; dry appropriately by line, flat or tumble; and iron at the correct temperature, pressing on the wrong side where possible. Bleach must be used with care - chlorine bleach on wool and silk destroys them - and fabric conditioners reduce absorbency, which matters on towels and sportswear. Whites and light colours are washed separately from darks, which prevents colour transfer, and new dark garments are washed alone the first time.

Stains are removed by treating them while fresh and knowing the stain's nature. Water-based stains such as fruit juice, tea, blood (cold water only, since heat sets protein stains) and mud lift with cold water and detergent; grease stains such as oil, butter and salad dressing need absorbent powder first and then a solvent or grease-removing detergent; ballpoint ink, rust, curry and grass respond to specific treatments such as methylated spirit, lemon juice or a proprietary spot remover. The rule is to blot, not rub; work from the outside of the stain inwards; test on a hidden seam allowance first; and never use hot water or iron on an unidentified stain, because heat can set it permanently. Storage protects the work: garments should be clean, dry, insect free and hung or folded to avoid strain, knitwear stored flat, whites wrapped away from light to prevent yellowing, and woollens protected from moths with clean, well-aired storage.
objectives: Interpret care-label symbols and choose a washing treatment for a fibre
Describe the correct order of laundering operations
Remove named stains correctly and explain how stains are set

experiment.description: Care Station: Read the fabric and the symbol, then choose the water temperature, detergent, drying and ironing.

lessons.title: Tools, Equipment and the Sewing Machine
lessons.content:
Textile work needs the right tools, kept sharp, clean and stored properly. Measuring tools include the tape measure, metre rule, hem gauge and seam gauge; marking tools include tailor's chalk, dressmaker's carbon and tracing wheel, washable pens and tacking thread; cutting tools include dressmaking shears for fabric, pinking shears for neatening, paper scissors, a seam ripper and pins; and sewing tools include hand needles for different threads, machine needles for different fabrics, thimbles, a needle threader and a bodkin. Pressing tools matter as much as sewing tools: a dry iron, a steam iron, a sleeve board, a pressing cloth, a tailor's ham and a seam roll allow seams to be pressed correctly rather than flattened. Cutting paper with shears, using a needle too fine for the thread, or pressing without a cloth are the commonest avoidable faults.

The sewing machine must be understood before it can be used well. The main parts are the spool pin and thread guides, the tension discs, the take-up lever, the needle clamp and needle, the presser foot and its lever, the feed dogs that move the fabric, the throat plate, the bobbin case and bobbin winder, the balance or hand wheel, the stitch length and width selectors, and the reverse lever. Threading follows a fixed route from spool to needle, and the bobbin thread is raised before stitching begins. Correct threading, matching needle and thread weight to the fabric, thread tension balanced between top and bobbin, and a correct stitch length are the four conditions for a good stitch.

Faults are diagnosed from their appearance. Loops underneath the fabric mean the top tension is too loose or the machine is not threaded correctly; loops on top mean the bobbin tension or bobbin winding is at fault; skipped stitches usually mean a blunt or wrong needle, or the needle is not fully up in the clamp; broken needles mean pulling the fabric, thick fabric being forced, or the needle hitting a pin; puckered seams mean tight tension or a needle too large for fine fabric; and a noisy, stiff machine needs cleaning and oiling. Regular maintenance - brushing lint from the feed dogs and bobbin case, oiling according to the manual, never running the machine with the presser foot down and no fabric, and covering or storing it correctly - keeps it reliable. The overlocker (serger) trims and neatens an edge in one pass, and its threads and cutting blades need their own care.
objectives: Identify, use and care for measuring, marking, cutting and sewing tools
Name the parts of the sewing machine and thread it correctly
Diagnose common stitching faults and carry out routine maintenance

experiment.description: Machine Doctor: Match each stitching fault to its cause and set the correct tension or needle.

lessons.title: Hand and Machine Stitches for Construction
lessons.content:
Stitches hold fabric together and are described as temporary or permanent, and as hand or machine worked. Temporary stitches - tacking, basting and tailor's tacks - hold layers, mark and transfer pattern lines and are removed once the permanent stitching is done. Permanent hand stitches include running stitch for gathering and seams, backstitch for strong seams on firm fabric, hemming for invisible edges, slip stitch for closing openings and attaching linings, and blanket and overcasting stitches for neatening raw edges. Decorative hand stitches - chain, stem, satin, cross and feather stitch - are used as trimming rather than construction.

Machine stitching is faster and more uniform. A straight stitch joins seams, a zigzag stitch neatens raw edges and can be used for stretch fabrics and buttonholes, a stretch or three-step zigzag follows knit without snapping, blind hem stitching finishes hems on soft fabrics, and overlock stitching trims and neatens together. Whatever the method, the stitch must suit the fabric: fine needles and short stitches for fine fabric, a heavier needle and longer stitch for denim and canvas, and a ballpoint needle for knits.

Seams are the backbone of garment construction. The plain (open) seam is pressed open and the raw edges are neatened separately; the flat fell seam encases both raw edges and is used where strength and a neat inside finish are needed, as on jeans; the French seam encloses the raw edges inside a fold and is used on fine fabrics and sheer curtains; and the run-and-fell and overlaid seams are used on children's clothes and workwear. Neatening may be by zigzag, overlocking, pinking, binding with a strip of fabric or turning and stitching. Other construction features build on the seam: darts shape the fabric to the body, gathers and pleats control fullness, tucks are decorative and functional, and hems finish the lower edges of garments - turned, faced, bias-bound or rolled depending on the fabric and the shape. Fastenings complete the garment: buttons and buttonholes, hooks and eyes or bars, press studs, zips (concealed, centred and lapped), velcro and decorative ties each suit particular openings and fabric weights.
objectives: Select and work temporary, permanent and decorative stitches
Describe seam types and choose one for a given fabric and purpose
Explain darts, gathers, hems and the common fastenings

experiment.description: Seam Chooser: Pick the fabric and the garment area, then choose the correct seam, neatening and fastening.

lessons.title: Taking Measurements, Pattern Reading and Fitting
lessons.content:
Good fit starts with accurate measurement. Body measurements are taken over light clothing with the tape snug but not tight and read to the nearest half centimetre, with the client standing naturally. The essential measurements are bust or chest, waist, hip, nape-to-waist length (for bodices), back and front waist lengths, shoulder width, and for skirts and trousers the skirt or trouser length, crotch depth and inseam. Sleeve length, armhole, neck, and calf or thigh measurements are added for a complete set. Consistency matters more than any single reading: the same landmarks, the same tension on the tape and the same posture every time, because a garment drafted on wrong measurements will not fit no matter how well it is sewn.

A paper pattern is a set of pieces with markings that stand for the shape and the construction. The symbols are standard: the grain line arrow must run parallel to the fabric selvedge; the notches match pieces together; the dart lines shape the garment; the fold line is placed on a fold; the place-on-fold arrow does the same; stitch lines and cutting lines are separated by a seam allowance; and the pattern pieces carry the size, the name, and the number of pieces to cut. Pattern envelopes give size charts, the body measurements used (not the finished garment measurements), fabric required for each width, notions and suggested fabrics, and they should be checked before buying the cloth. Commercial patterns are multi-sized, but the pattern size is not the ready-to-wear size, so the body measurement chart decides.

Pattern layout and cutting must respect the fabric. The fabric is straightened by pulling a weft thread and cutting along it, then pressed, then folded right sides together with selvedges matching; pieces are pinned with the grain line true to the selvedge and with a nap or one-way design all running the same way; the layout diagram on the instruction sheet saves fabric; and the allowance is cut or notched at the edges. Fitting is finding and correcting problems on the body or a toile: the common faults are a bodice too tight across the bust or too loose at the neckline, gaping armholes, a waistline that sits too high or low, darts that point away from the bust apex instead of towards it, a shoulder that is too wide or narrow, sleeves that twist, a skirt that rides up at the back, and a hem that is uneven because of posture. Each has a fix - letting out or taking in at the seam, moving the dart apex, adjusting the shoulder seam, or re-marking and re-levelling the hem.
objectives: Take a complete and accurate set of body measurements
Read pattern markings, envelope information and size charts
Lay out, cut and fit a simple garment, correcting common fitting faults

experiment.description: Fit Finder: Enter body and garment measurements and identify the fitting fault and its correction.

lessons.title: The Elements and Principles of Design
lessons.content:
Design is planned arrangement, and good design uses defined elements and principles. The elements are line, shape, form, colour, texture, space and pattern. Line gives direction and mood: vertical lines lengthen and slim, horizontal lines widen and emphasise, diagonal and curved lines add movement and softness, and the dominant line of a garment is usually the seam or neckline that runs across its structure. Shape and form describe the silhouette - A-line, straight, fitted, empire, tent or hourglass. Texture is the visual and tactile quality of the fabric, from crisp cotton to soft jersey or nubby linen. Pattern may be floral, geometric, abstract or traditional, and Caribbean design draws on bright tropical colour, madras checks, batik and carnival imagery.

The principles organise those elements: balance (symmetrical or asymmetrical), rhythm (repetition and gradation that lead the eye), proportion (the relationship of one part to another and to the whole), emphasis (a focal point such as a collar, belt or appliqué), harmony and unity (all parts working together), and contrast (light against dark, texture against smooth). A design succeeds when the principles are used deliberately: a trim used three times creates rhythm; a single dramatic sleeve creates emphasis; and a print kept in proportion to the wearer prevents the fabric overwhelming the person.

Colour is the element with the strongest effect, and colour theory gives the maker control over it. The colour wheel organises primary colours (red, blue, yellow), secondary colours made from them and tertiary colours between. Harmonies include monochromatic (one hue in several values), analogous (neighbouring hues), complementary (opposite hues, which intensify each other) and split complementary and triadic schemes. Hue is the colour itself, value is its lightness or darkness (a tint is a lighter value, a shade darker), and intensity is its brightness. Warm colours advance and cool colours recede, so a warm colour on an area draws the eye; dark values appear to reduce size and light values increase it. The same logic applies to line and pattern, which is why a design should be chosen for its effect on the wearer's own proportions, colouring and occasion rather than on the trend alone.
objectives: Identify the elements and principles of design in a garment
Use line, texture and pattern deliberately to create an effect
Apply colour theory and colour effects to a personal design

experiment.description: Design Studio: Build a garment on a figure by choosing line, colour, texture and pattern and see the visual effect.

lessons.title: Constructing a Garment: Order of Work and Finishing
lessons.content:
Efficient making is a matter of sequence. The order of work for a simple garment is: read the pattern instructions and plan the tasks; adjust and cut the pattern; straighten, press and lay out the fabric; cut, mark and transfer all pattern lines; stay-stitch and interface where needed; make the darts; join the shoulder seams; attach the collar or facings; set in or attach the sleeves; join the side seams and underarm seams; attach the fastening or zip; attach the waistband, yoke or band if there is one; neaten all raw edges; level and stitch the hem; make the buttonholes and buttons or other fastening finish; and give the final press. Written down as a production plan with a time estimate for each step, this becomes the record of work that practical assessment requires.

Some features need special technique. Interfacing stiffens and stabilises collars, cuffs, waistbands and buttonhole areas; it is fusible (ironed on) or sew-in, and must be chosen to match the weight of the fabric. Collars and facings are sewn, trimmed, graded, clipped at curves, turned and pressed so that the seam rolls slightly to the underside and does not show. Sleeves are set in flat or on a curved armhole; the sleeve head is eased in with one or two rows of gathering thread, and any puff or gather is distributed evenly. Zips must be positioned so that the fabric does not pucker: for a lapped or centred zip the seam allowances are tacked, the zip is pinned and stitched from the right side with a zip foot, and the tacking is removed afterwards. Waistbands and bands are interfaced, applied, trimmed and under-stitched so that the band does not roll. Gathers are drawn up evenly to a measured length, pleats are pinned and tacked before stitching, and pockets must be positioned to match on both sides and reinforced at the openings.

Finishing is what separates a homemade garment from a made one. Every raw edge should be neatened and no loose thread should remain inside; hems should be level, evenly turned and invisibly stitched; fastenings should lie flat and work smoothly; and the garment should be pressed throughout, not only at the end. Pressing is done as you sew - press the seam before crossing it with another seam, press darts over a ham, press curved seams over a seam roll, use a damp cloth on cotton and linen, and lift and place the iron rather than pushing it over the fabric. Irons are also a hazard: never iron a garment with pins in it, never leave a hot iron face down or unattended, and keep the cable clear of the work. A final check asks the four questions assessors ask: does it fit, is it well sewn, is it well pressed, and is it finished inside as neatly as outside?
objectives: Write a logical order of work and a production plan for a simple garment
Construct named features correctly, including interfacing, collars, sleeves and zips
Press and finish a garment to a professional standard

experiment.description: Production Planner: Put the construction steps in the correct order and allocate time to build a plan.

lessons.title: Decorative Techniques and Embellishment
lessons.content:
Decoration should enhance a garment without spoiling its line, comfort or care. Appliqué is the application of one fabric on top of another, stitched around the shape with machine satin stitch, hand blanket stitch or zigzag, and it can create lettering, motifs, patches and pictorial designs; edges may be raw, turned or fused, and vliesofix backing keeps small pieces crisp. Embroidery uses needle and thread to add surface pattern: counted-thread work such as cross stitch, free work such as satin, chain and stem stitch, cutwork and drawn thread, and the pulled work and lace that use the fabric's own structure. Smocking uses evenly spaced rows of gathering - usually honeycomb or cable stitch - to control fullness and let knit or stretched fabric give, and it is traditional on children's clothes and peasant blouses.

Dyeing and printing add colour to fabric or yarn. Tie-dye resists colour where fabric is tied, knotted or bound; batik resists with wax that is painted or stamped on and melted off afterwards, and both are strongly associated with Caribbean craft because the effects suit bright colour and simple shapes. Wax and paste resist, block and screen printing and stencilling are the other main approaches. Quilting stitches layers together with wadding between them for warmth and texture, patchwork joins pieces into new fabric, and both recycle otherwise unusable scraps. Trimmings - bias binding, piping, braid, lace, rickrack, buttons, beadwork, sequins and ribbons - finish edges and add emphasis, and a design that relies on trimmings must still be washable and comfortable.

Decoration has rules, mostly about restraint and care. The technique must suit the fabric: heavy beading distorts fine fabric and appliqué on a stretch knit must stretch with it. Decoration should be placed to enhance the design's focal point, be balanced on both sides where symmetry is intended, be strong enough to survive washing, and never be added where it interferes with pressing, fastenings or fit. It should be removable or washable where the garment is to be laundered often, and any threads or beads must be secured so that wear does not unravel the design. Kept within these limits, decoration is where a maker's skill and a Caribbean sense of colour and pattern become visible - and where a plain garment becomes personal.
objectives: Choose a decorative technique that suits the fabric and the design
Work appliqué, embroidery, smocking or a resist-dye technique correctly
Apply trimmings and embellishment so that the garment stays wearable and washable

experiment.description: Decorate It: Choose a fabric and a design area, then pick the decoration and check it survives washing.

title: Textiles in the Home, Consumer Skills and Enterprise

lessons.title: Consumer Skills and the Clothing Market
lessons.content:
A consumer is anyone who buys or uses goods and services, and a clothing consumer has both rights and responsibilities. The basic rights are the right to safety, to be informed, to choose and to be heard; in the Caribbean these are protected by consumer protection acts, standards bureaux, fair trading and bureau of standards legislation, and by organisations that handle complaints. Responsibilities include buying wisely, reading labels, keeping receipts, making complaints properly, and being honest about a fault caused by misuse or normal wear rather than by manufacture.

Wise buying is a process. The buyer identifies the need and the purpose - school, church, work, sport, a special occasion - and sets a budget; compares quality, price and the cost per wear rather than the price tag alone; checks fibre content, care instructions, seam quality, stitching, hems, fastenings, pattern matching and fit; asks about the shop's returns policy before buying; and keeps the receipt. Ready-made clothing is convenient and often cheaper, but handmade garments allow perfect fit, better quality and individual style at the cost of time and skill; mending and altering existing clothes is the cheapest option of all. Consumers should also recognise selling tactics: the hard sell, the discount that was never a real price, the pressure of a limited-time offer, and the practice of buying on credit that converts a low price into a high total.

Everybody in the market buys under labels and brands, and labels carry information that the buyer must be able to use: fibre content percentages, size, country of origin, manufacturer or importer, prescribed care instructions, and any safety information such as flame-resistance warnings. The cost of a garment to the consumer is more than its price: it includes the cost of care over its life (water, detergent, electricity, ironing and dry cleaning), the number of years it will last, and the environmental cost of the fibre and the production process. Garments made from natural fibres and well-constructed garments, though dearer up front, often cost less per wear. Reading labels and comparing workmanship are the two habits that make a consumer hard to cheat and reliably well dressed.
objectives: State the rights and responsibilities of the Caribbean clothing consumer
Apply the steps of wise buying and compare ready-made, handmade and altered garments
Interpret garment labels and evaluate cost per wear and total cost

experiment.description: Shopping Round: Compare three garments on label, workmanship and cost per wear and choose the best buy.

lessons.title: Soft Furnishings and Textiles in the Home
lessons.content:
Textiles do much more than dress the body: they shape the comfort, hygiene and appearance of the home. In the bedroom they are bed linen, duvet covers, pillowcases, blankets, mattress covers and bedspreads; in the living room they are curtains, cushions, throws, upholstery and wall hangings; in the kitchen and dining area they are tablecloths, napkins, runners, tea towels, aprons and oven gloves; in the bathroom they are towels and bath mats; and throughout the house they are mats, rugs, lamp shades and storage bags and baskets. Each item makes demands on the fabric chosen: bed linen and towels need absorbency and durability, upholstery needs abrasion resistance and fade resistance, kitchen textiles need heat resistance and easy washing, bathroom textiles need quick drying and mildew resistance, and curtains need drape, sun resistance and the ability to hold a fold.

Measuring and making soft furnishings is applied textile skill. Curtains are hung on a track or pole, and the finished width should be one and a half to two and a half times the window width for the chosen heading (pencil pleat, pinch pleat, eyelet, tab top or gathered), with the finished length measuring from the top of the heading to the hem, plus hems and heading allowance. Fabric is cut with the pattern matched across the joins, curtains are lined or interlined where the fabric needs protection from sun or where privacy and insulation matter, and the hem is made deep and weighted so the curtain hangs straight. Cushion covers are made with an envelope, zip or button opening and often have piping or a trim; table linen needs true right angles and mitred corners so it hangs evenly; and a fitted or flat sheet, a duvet cover and a pillowcase follow the same principles of measuring twice and sewing accurately. Household items should also be designed for the people who use them - washable, safe, and free of trims that could catch or burn.

Textiles in the home must be cared for and are a household expense to plan for. Items are rotated and inspected, mended before they split, washed according to the fibre, dried thoroughly to prevent mildew in humid Caribbean conditions, and stored with protection against damp, insects and dust. Choosing textiles thoughtfully and repairing them extends their life, saves money, and reduces the volume of fabric and furnishing waste a household sends to the dump - which is where personal care and sustainability meet.
objectives: Select suitable fabrics for named household textiles based on their demands
Measure and make a simple soft furnishing such as a curtain or cushion cover
Explain the care, repair and cost of household textiles

experiment.description: Room Planner: Choose the room and the item, then select the fibre, the measurements and the care plan.

lessons.title: The Fashion Industry, Enterprise and Careers
lessons.content:
Clothing and textiles are a major industry as well as a craft. The fashion industry runs from fibre production and textile manufacture to design, pattern making, sampling, manufacturing, wholesale, retailing, marketing, and after-sales services such as alteration and repair, with auxiliary industries in machinery, threads, trims, packaging and education. Caribbean economies have a long history in textiles - sugar bags, tobacco and crop wrappers, cotton and garment assembly for export - and today the region's strengths are in design-led small business, carnival and festival costume production, uniforms for schools and hotels, craft textiles, and boutique tourism-linked clothing and accessories.

Enterprise begins with costing and pricing a product. The cost of making one garment includes direct materials (fabric, thread, interfacing, zips, buttons, trims, pattern) and direct labour (the time at an honest wage), plus overheads allocated per item (machine maintenance, electricity, rent, equipment, insurance, transport, packaging) and any selling costs (market stall or booth fees, commissions, advertising). Mark-up is added to that unit cost to give a selling price, and the maker must compare the price with what the market will pay; if the market price is below the cost, the design, the batch size, the supplier or the wage assumptions must change. A simple cost sheet, a price list and records of sales and expenses are the minimum bookkeeping, and they matter because most small textile businesses fail on pricing and record-keeping rather than on sewing.

Marketing a textile business means knowing the customer and reaching them: producing a small range rather than one-offs, photographing garments well, using social media, markets, fairs and craft shows, taking orders for school and uniform contracts, offering alterations and repairs, and building a reputation for quality and delivery on time. Careers in the field are broader than sewing: fashion designer, pattern maker, sample machinist, tailor, dressmaker, alteration hand, embroiderer, milliner, costume maker, upholsterer, textile artist, printer or dyer, retail buyer or sales assistant, visual merchandiser, quality controller, textile technologist, teacher, pattern grader, and business owner. Apprenticeships, national training agencies, community colleges and small-business support programmes are the usual routes into them, and the same skills support earning at home while studying - which is exactly how many Caribbean makers begin.
objectives: Describe the stages of the fashion industry from fibre to retail
Prepare a cost sheet and set a selling price for a garment
Identify textile careers and ways to market a small textile business

experiment.description: Cost Sheet: Enter materials, labour time and overheads and see the unit cost, mark-up and break-even number of garments.

lessons.title: Safety, Hygiene and First Aid in the Workroom
lessons.content:
A textile workroom contains sharp, hot and fast-moving hazards, and most accidents come from rushing, untidiness or taking short cuts. The main risks are cuts from shears, scissors, rotary cutters, pins and rippers; needle and pin pricks under the skin, and broken needles flying; burns and fires from irons, steam and pressing equipment; fingers being caught by the machine needle or the belt and wheel; electric shock from damaged cords and overloaded sockets; eye injury from flying pins or sparks; strain injuries from poor posture and long hours at the machine; and dust, fibre and chemical exposure from fabric, lint, dyes and solvents.

Control measures are simple and consistent. Keep the work area clean, dry and well lit, with a padded chair at the right height and a footrest so the back is straight and the wrists neutral; store tools in a box or pouch with needles in a pin cushion and never in the mouth or pinned to clothing; cut away from the body and pass scissors handle first; keep fingers clear of the needle and always watch the needle, not the fabric edge; switch off and unplug the machine before threading, changing the needle, oiling or cleaning, and never run it with the presser foot down and no fabric; stand the iron on its heel or on the rack, never face down on the board, never leave it unattended, and keep the cable away from the walkway; do not pin over a seam about to be stitched and remove pins as you go; and wear an apron, closed shoes and tied-back hair. Chemical products - dyes, bleach, solvents and fabric adhesives - are stored in labelled containers, used in ventilated space with gloves, kept away from heat and never mixed.

Hygiene and first aid complete the picture. Hands are washed before handling fabric and food-related textiles; garments in progress are stored clean and away from pets, food and floor dust; and pressing cloths and needles are kept clean, because dirty tools mark work. When an accident happens the response is immediate: stop the machine or equipment, keep calm, and treat - wash and cover a cut, apply pressure if it bleeds heavily, and send for medical help if the injury is deep; cool a burn under running water for at least twenty minutes and never apply butter, oil or ointment; keep a person still and do not pull a needle out if the eye or a joint is involved, but seek medical help; switch off and isolate the power before touching anyone in an electrical accident, and do not touch the casualty until the current is off; and report and record every accident so that the cause can be corrected. A well-run room also displays the safety rules, the emergency numbers and the first-aid box where everyone can see them.
objectives: Identify the hazards of a textile workroom and the control measures for each
Work safely and hygienically with tools, machines, irons and chemicals
Apply correct first-aid responses to cuts, burns, needle injury and electric shock

experiment.description: Workroom Safety Scan: Inspect the room, spot the hazards and choose the correct control and first-aid response.

lessons.title: Sustainable Textiles and Reducing Waste
lessons.content:
Sustainability means meeting present needs without spoiling the ability of future generations to meet theirs, and the clothing industry is one of the largest environmental pressures in the world. Problems include the water and pesticides used to grow cotton, the energy and chemicals used in dyeing and finishing, the petrochemical origin and slow degradation of synthetic fibres, the greenhouse gases and microplastics released in washing, the volumes of unsold stock destroyed, and the waste of short-life factory-made fashion - the fast-fashion cycle in which clothes are bought cheaply, worn briefly and discarded. Textile waste in landfills releases methane and sheds microfibres, and much of it is usable material.

The maker and the consumer both have leverage. Reduce means buying less and better: fewer garments, chosen well, repaired rather than replaced, and cared for so that they last. Reuse means passing clothes on, swapping, buying second-hand or vintage, restyling outdated garments, cutting down adult clothing for children, and using worn fabric for quilts, patchwork, bags, cushion covers, dusters and rags. Recycle means returning fibre for reprocessing, using textile recycling schemes, and choosing recycled polyester, regenerated cellulosics or deadstock fabric. In production, waste is cut by planning the layout to use the minimum fabric, keeping a scrap box for small projects, cutting facings, bindings and interfacings from leftovers, and saving sample and toile fabric for practice.

Eco-friendlier choices need honest evaluation. Organic cotton reduces pesticide use; linen and hemp need little irrigation; lyocell and Tencel use closed-loop solvents; bamboo viscose is often processed with harsh chemicals despite the plant's image; natural dyes and low-water dyeing reduce pollution but may fade faster; and local, small-batch production cuts transport but not waste. There is no single perfect fibre, so the maker weighs water, energy, chemistry, durability and end-of-life, and specifies the material to suit the product and the local climate, where cotton and linen are appropriate for comfort and synthetics better judged for swimwear and rainwear. Sustainability also has a social face: fair pay, safe factories, no child labour and honest labelling in supply chains, and a Caribbean market that buys from local designers keeps money and skills in the region.
objectives: Describe the environmental problems of textile production and consumption
Apply the reduce, reuse and recycle hierarchy to fabric and clothing
Evaluate fibre choices for environmental impact and social fairness

experiment.description: Waste Audit: Tally the fabric, water and waste in a garment's life and find the biggest saving.

lessons.title: Caribbean Textiles, Craft and Cultural Identity
lessons.content:
Textiles carry Caribbean history and identity. Before and after European contact, indigenous peoples used cotton, palm, bark, sisal and beads; the plantation economy then tied the region to cloth - coarse osnaburg and check fabric for enslaved people, madras and bandana cloth brought through trade with India for use in head ties and working dress, and the market and haberdashery trade that grew up around Caribbean towns. Emancipation and migration added new traditions, including the tucking, embroidery and pleating of cotton in the Leeward and Windward Islands, and the intricate lace-like needlework and patchwork that travelled with indentured workers and their descendants. Traditional dress - the head tie, the full skirt and the madras plaid - survives in folk performance, national dress and festivals.

Carnival and festival culture is the region's largest textile enterprise. Costume makers build wire, cane and foam frames, cover them with fabric, sequins, jewels, feathers and beads, and produce hundreds of costumes for masquerade bands each year, with skills in pattern cutting, beading, spraying and construction that are rarely taught formally but are passed on in the yard. Alongside this are the craft textiles: straw and palm weaving for hats, mats, bags and brooms; coir and sisal work; batik and tie-dyed cloth; silk-screened and hand-painted T-shirts; leather sandals and belts; embroidery and appliqué; and the crochet, knitting and craft items that support handicraft markets and tourist trade.

Cultural identity and economic opportunity meet in the modern Caribbean textile sector. Local designers use madras, calico, batik, crochet and hand-dyed cloth in contemporary garments, and their work signals a deliberate choice of local material and local imagery over imported fashion. Opportunities lie in school and hotel uniforms, costumes, souvenirs, boutique fashion, upcycling, online selling and export under regional trade arrangements; challenges lie in competition from cheap imports, the cost of raw materials, access to finance, machinery and training, and the small size of domestic markets. For a student, the practical value of the subject is that it links a craft to a livelihood: skills learned for the SBA - designing, costing, making, marketing and recording - are the same skills a small textile business needs, and the region's festivals, hotels and diaspora provide customers for them.
objectives: Describe the historical development of Caribbean textile traditions
List the main Caribbean textile crafts and carnival costume techniques
Explain the opportunities and challenges facing local designers and craft producers

experiment.description: Craft Map: Match each Caribbean island or community to its textile craft, material and market.
